background.definition: Hodgkin's lymphoma (HL), previously known as Hodgkin's disease, is marked by the presence of a type of cell called the Reed-Sternberg cell and is clinically characterized by the spread of disease to lymph nodes, lymphoid tissues, and extralymphatic organs such as the spleen, liver, bone marrow, and lung. The World Health Organization classification includes nodular lymphocyte-predominant HL and classical HL. The latter is subdivided into nodular sclerosis HL, mixed-cellularity HL, lymphocyte depletion HL, and lymphocyte-rich classical HL.

list.listitem: Estimated 8200 new cases and 1100 deaths in the United States in 2007.
Male/female ratio: 1.4:1.
The estimated prevalence in the United States in 2004 was 150,000 patients (78,000 male and 73,000 female).

In a cost utility analysis, the average effective costs per survivor were 8827 Euro for intensive care unit costs and 14,130 Euro for intensive care unit and hospital costs. Mean costs per life year and per quality-adjusted life year gained amounted to 19,330 Euro and 21,922 Euro, respectively.
HL is the third most common cancer in the 15- to 29-year-old age group.
HL comprises 6% of childhood cancers.
Only 10% to 15% of all cases occur in patients younger than 16 years.

A striking male/female predominance is found among young children, with a ratio of 4:1 for 3- to 7-year-olds, and 3:1 for 7- to 9-year-olds. For patients older than 10 years, the ratio is 1.3:1 (a ratio more similar to that of adults).
The cause of HL is unknown.
Susceptibility to specific viral oncogenes or certain human leukocyte antigen subtypes suggest a multifactorial etiology with a genetic influence.
Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) genetic material can often be detected in the affected cells.
There is a 7-fold increase in the development of HL in siblings of parents with a history of this malignancy. Risk is also increased in smokers.
HL is characterized by the presence of multinucleated giant cells, called Reed-Sternberg cells, or mononuclear giant cells, called Hodgkin's cells.
HL typically arises in B cells that cannot synthesize immunoglobulin and are resistant to apoptosis.
Common symptoms include lymph node swelling, fever, night sweats, and weight loss. C
Open biopsy of enlarged lymph nodes to show the presence of Hodgkin's or Reed-Sternberg cells is mandatory. B
For staging, or extent of disease, perform a complete blood work-up, blood chemistry, ESR, CXR, and CT scan of the neck, chest, pelvis, and abdomen. B
MRI, PET scans, and bone marrow biopsy may also be needed. C

Differential.Differential_Features: More likely to have sore throat, headache, and rash usually lasting no more than 1 month. Lymph node biopsy is negative for Reed-Sternberg and Hodgkin's cells
More likely to have flu-like illness and rash. Positive serum HIV antibody and negative lymph node biopsy for Reed-Sternberg and Hodgkin's cells
More likely to have painless, matted cervical nodes. Positive PPD and negative lymph node biopsy for Reed-Sternberg and Hodgkin's cells
Presence of arthritis and serum rheumatoid factor. Negative lymph node biopsy for Reed-Sternberg and Hodgkin's cells
More likely to have pulmonary symptoms. Presence of noncaseating granulomas on biopsy. Negative lymph node biopsy for Reed-Sternberg and Hodgkin's cells
Absence of Reed-Sternberg cells is characteristic for NHL. B symptoms are more common in HL at the time of diagnosis
More likely to have symptoms that reflect bone marrow involvement including anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia. Negative lymph node biopsy for Reed-Sternberg and Hodkin's cells

list.listitem: HL is definitively diagnosed and categorized through histologic examination of a lymph node.
The staging system for HL is the Ann Arbor system ().

There are some symptoms for HL, but they are not specific. Patients usually present with peripheral, nontender, freely movable lymphadenopathies mostly located in the cervical and supraclavicular region (60%-80%). Axillary and inguinal-femoral presentations are less common.

Malignant lymphadenopathy is more likely with larger nodes, a greater number of sites of lymphadenopathy, supraclavicular location, fixed nodes, duration of greater than 2 weeks, and nodal tenderness.

Use of a short course of antibiotics or corticosteroids in the patient with unexplained lymphadenopathy is common practice. However, there is no evidence to support this practice, which should be avoided because it may hinder or delay diagnosis.
Mediastinal involvement may occur without local symptoms. Retrosternal chest pain, cough, or shortness of breath may be clinical signs of intrathoracic disease.

Ascites and abdominal swelling are rarely seen; signs of abdominal disease including hepatic and splenic involvement may be present. Approximately 30% of patients with clinical stage I to II disease will have involvement of the spleen, abdominal nodes, or liver at laparotomy.Palpation of the spleen on examination strongly increases the likelihood of splenomegaly.
Infradiaphragmatic lymphadenopathy may give rise to discomfort and pain.

Other noteworthy symptoms are B symptoms: (1) loss of more than 10% of body weight over the previous 6 months, (2) fever of 38°C or greater without any known cause, and (3) drenching night sweats. These symptoms increase in frequency from 8% of patient with stage I to 68% of those with stage IV disease. Fever and drenching night sweats are found in 25% of all patients at time of presentation.
Fewer than 20% of patients have itching and some patients have a lower back pain that is unexplained. (Lower back pain may be caused by growing lymph nodes pressing on nerves.)
Involved nodes may be painful after alcohol consumption.

The purpose of the diagnostic evaluation is to define the extent of the disease. A CBC with a differential, blood chemistries, and ESR are baseline laboratory tests. Abnormal blood count, elevated alkaline phosphatase or lactate dehydrogenase levels, or an elevated ESR may be the harbinger of bone marrow involvement. The International Prognostic Index (IPI) predicts overall survival and includes low serum albumin and Hb levels, leukocytosis, and lymphopenia as prognostic factors.
Perform a CXR in all patients to view mediastinal lymph nodes and to see whether other organs are involved.
Perform CT scan of the chest, pelvis, and abdomen to determine possible spread of the disease to paraaortic nodes, mediastinum and elsewhere.

MRI, PET, and bone marrow biopsy are additional useful tests to define the extent of the disease. MRI may be an alternative to chest or abdominal CT. It is more sensitive but less specific than CT to define the extent of abdominal disease.

PET scans can help determine whether an enlarged lymph node contains HL or is benign. In the few studies that have compared CT and PET staging of lymphoma, the sensitivities of the two modalities have been comparable. PET appears to be superior in treatment monitoring, particularly in distinguishing between residual viable tumor and fibrosis.

Bone marrow involvement is rare in patients with HL, and its incidence varies between 4% and 14%. Bone marrow biopsy and aspiration is required if B symptom are present or if the WBC is less than 4.0 x 109/L, or the hemoglobin is less than 12.0 g/dL (women) 13.0 g/dL (men,) or the platelets are less than 125 x 109/L.
With modern diagnostic tools available, laparotomy and lymphangiogram are rarely used.
Obtain a complete history for systemic symptoms (B symptoms) and examine all lymph node sites.
Establish the diagnosis by lymph node biopsy; aspiration cytology alone is not adequate.
If the biopsy reveals HL, determine the stage by CXR, CT and MRI of the neck, chest, pelvis, and abdomen, CBC, chemistries, and ESR.
Additional tests to determine extent of disease: PET scans, bone marrow biopsy, and aspiration.

Design treatment according to the stage of the disease, adverse risk factors, and International Prognostic Index. The main types of treatment are combination chemotherapy (ChT) and radiotherapy (RT). B Early favorable HL: combination ChT for 4 to 6 cycles, or combination ChT for 2 cycles plus RT. A Early unfavorable HL: 4 cycles of combination ChT plus RT or 4 to 6 cycles of combination ChT. A Advanced favorable HL: combination ChT for 6 to 8 cycles, or combination ChT for 6 to 8 cycles plus RT for some patients with bulky disease. A Advanced unfavorable HL: combination ChT for 6 to 8 cycles. A
Staging laparotomy is no longer recommended; it should be considered only when the results will allow substantial reduction in treatment.
It should not be done in patients who require chemotherapy.
Compared with nonfatigued persons, those with chronic fatigue are most likely to use body-based and mind-body therapies.
Some complementary therapies, from vitamins and herbal therapies to massage and acupuncture, may be helpful for patients with HL to relieve the side effects of conventional therapies.
Because many complementary and alternative therapies have not yet been studied, it is not known which are potentially helpful and which are potentially harmful.
Studies commonly focus on chronic fatigue of HL survivors.
In a pilot study, fatigue, physical functioning, and maximal aerobic capacity were significantly improved after home-based exercise intervention.
Aerobic exercise had a positive effect upon chronic fatigue in HL.
Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) uses a multimodal approach toward symptom management and is particularly effective in decreasing symptom severity for patients with cancer.
Most studies have tested the effectiveness of CBT in reducing the severity of the fatigue or pain.
There are no studies of CBT focused particularly on patients with HL.

The primary treatment modality for HL is the combination of chemotherapy and radiation therapy. A systematic review of 5 RCTs found significantly better event free and overall survival with combined treatment compared with chemotherapy alone.

An updated Cochrane review addressing combined modality therapy in early stage HL included 3840 patients across 8 RCTs. In favourable early stage disease the evidence was moderate for improved progression-free survival with the addition of radiotherapy to chemotherapy without any clear difference in risk of second cancer or cardiac complications.

Treatment of HL depends on the stage of the disease, adverse risk factors, and the International Prognostic Index. The size of the enlarged lymph nodes, which symptoms are present, and the age and general health of the patient are also important. The main types of treatment are chemotherapy as a combination of agents, radiation therapy, and bone marrow and peripheral blood transplants.

For advanced and unfavorable disease, chemotherapy is used for a longer duration than those used in early and favorable disease. Patients are classified into 4 subgroups, and treatment is chosen according to these groups (). A recent RCT found that 6 cycles of BEACOPP was as effective as 8 cycles, and that PET scan may be helpful to identify the need for further radiotherapy.

The German Hodgkins trial HD18 demonstrated that in advanced stage HL, a negative PET after 2 cycles BEACOPP enabled reduction to total of 4 cycles rather than 6 , without any loss of tumour control and with reduction in toxicity.

In patients with early unfavorable HL, a randomized trial with 1528 patients found that 2 cycles BEACOPP followed by 2 cycles ABVD reduced freedom from treatment failure compared with 4 cycles of ABVD (both arms received involved field radiotherapy), hazard ratio 0.44, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.66. The combination was more toxic, but treatment associated mortality was similar.

A Cochrane review comparing standard ABVD chemotherapy with escalated BEACOPP in early unfavorable or advanced stage patients demonstrates a clear survival benefit for BEACOPP. However, this is a more toxic regimen and the outcomes on second malignancy and fertility are not yet available.

Recent trials have focused on response-adapted therapy for HL intensifying or de-escalating chemotherapy based on early interim PET scan assessment of response after the first 2 cycles of chemotherapy. The SWOG S0186 used early PET as part of a response-adapted strategy in patients with stage III/IV HL. Five year follow up demonstrates a disappointingly high relapse rate in the PET negative group at 25%. In the PET positive group where chemotherapy was intensified to eBeaCOPP there was a high risk of second malignancy (14% versus 2%). This shows the need for ongoing trials to improve outcomes.

Brentuximab vedotin is being studied for patients with relapsed or recurrent HL, and after autologous stem cell transplant. It is a conjugate of the antibody and drug that targets the TNF receptor on cancer cells. A randomized trial of 1334 patients with stage III or IV Hodgkin's Lymphoma randomized them brentuximab vedotin, doxorubicin, vinblastine and dacarbazine OR doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, and dacarbazine. Updated 3 year follow-up shows progression free survival was 83% in the brentuximab group and 76% in the comparison group. There was durable efficacy with the use of brentuximab regardless of stage, prognositc risk factors or interim PET result. A 6 year median follow-up of the same study showed persistent benefit in terms of overall survival (93.9% vs 89.4%, p = 0.001, NNT = 22.

A more recent study, however, compared brentuximab-AVD (adriamycin,vinblastine, dacarbazine) with nivolumab-AVD in patients with advanced (stage III or IV) Hodgkin lymphoma with progression free survival as the primary outcome. Nivolumab is a form of immunotherapy shown to be effective in relapsed disease patients. With 970 patients in the trial 2 year progression free survival was higher with nivolumab combination than with brentuximab (92% vs 83%).

The HD21 phase 3 RCT with 1500 patients has also explored the use of brentuximab as part of combination chemotherapy in advanced stage Hodgkin lymphoma compared against standard eBEACOPP. While progression free survival improved in the brentuximab group and there was reduced toxicity compared to eBEACOPP, there is no difference in overall survival at 4 years.

A trial in 587 pediatric/young adult patients with Hodgkin's similarly suggests benefit from brentuxiamb compared to standard therapy in unfavorable patients as first line therapy with benefit in event free survival (92% vs 82%).

For recurrent disease, use reinduction with the same or another chemotherapy regimen followed by high-dose chemotherapy and autologous bone marrow or peripheral stem cell or allogenic bone marrow rescue.

Pembrolizumab in the Keynote 087 trial investigated efficacy across a variety of refractory cohorts who were progressing post ASCT or following salvage chemotherapy; this immunotherapy agent was found to be effective across all cohorts on 2 year follow-up.
The total duration of therapy depends on the stage of the disease and chemotherapy regimen, that is, 8 cycles of BEACOPP is 24 weeks compared with 32 weeks for 4 double cycles of COPP/ABVD.
In addition, 20 Gy of radiotherapy takes 2 weeks compared with 3 weeks for 30 Gy.
Side effects of treatment can include nausea (feeling sick) and vomiting, hair loss, increased risk of infection or bruising and bleeding, tiredness, and diarrhea.

Antibiotic prophylaxis in afebrile, neutropenic patients has been shown in a Cochrane systematic review to reduce all-cause mortality in a patient population with predominantly hematological malignancy.
Dental caries: neck or oropharyngeal irradiation may cause decreased salivation. Patients should have careful dental care follow-up.

Hypothyroidism: after external beam thyroid irradiation, at least 50% of patients will eventually become hypothyroid. There is an increased risk of secondary thyroid carcinoma. All patients whose thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level becomes elevated should be treated with life-long thyroxine replacement for 2 purposes: to maintain euthyroidism and to minimize the risk of thyroid carcinoma by reducing overstimulation with endogenous TSH.

Infertility: ABVD ChT and direct or scatter radiation to gonadal tissue may cause infertility, amenorrhea, or premature menopause. In general, after treatment, women who continue menstruating are fertile, but men require semen analysis to provide a specific answer.

Secondary neoplasms: acute myelogenous leukemia, thyroid, breast, lung, and upper GI carcinoma and melanoma, as well as cervical carcinoma in situ occur in patients who have been treated for HL. There is increasing evidence that single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNIPs) can predict patients at increased risk of specific neoplasms, for example FGFR2 and breast cancer following radiation.
Relapse: 10% to 30% of patients relapse. Careful attention should be directed to lymph node sites, especially if previously involved with disease.
Nontumor-directed therapeutic strategies include supportive interventions such as pain control, psychosocial aid, antiemesis, adequate control of infections, or nutritional support.
The 5-year relative overall survival rate is 84.9%. B
The 5- and 10-year event-free survival rates for early-stage HL are 82% to 98%. A
For advanced stage, the 5-year freedom-from-progression rate is 42% to 80%. A
HL begins in a single group of lymph nodes and then spreads to contiguous lymph nodes.

Eventually the malignant cells may become more aggressive, invade blood vessels, and spread to organs in a manner similar to that in other malignancies. This is more likely to occur in patients with stage III than with stage I or II HL.
The spleen is involved more frequently in patients with adenopathy below the diaphragm, systemic symptoms, and MC histologic type.
Involvement of the liver in an untreated patient is rare and almost always occurs with concomitant splenic involvement.
Infiltration of the bone marrow is usually focal and almost invariably associated with extensive disease and systemic symptoms.
In the great majority of patients, the initial pattern of spread occurs nonrandomly and predictably via lymphatic channels to contiguous lymph node chains.
The overall 5-year relative survival rate for 1996 to 2003 from 17 SEER geographic areas was 84.9%.
In patients between the ages of 15 years and 49 years, the 5-year relative survival rates were 87% in men and 92% in women, compared with 27% and 32%, respectively, in those older than 70 years.
HL survival rates tend to be a little better in women than in men.
The 5- and 10-year event-free rates were 98% and 93%, respectively, for early-stage favorable disease and 84% and 82%, respectively, for early-stage unfavorable disease.
For advanced favorable disease, the 5-year freedom-from-progression rate was 60% to 80%, and for advanced unfavorable disease it was 42% to 51%.
Adverse risk factors include B symptoms, extranodal disease, bulky disease, 3 or more sites of nodal involvement, and an ESR of 50 or higher.
A ratio at diagnosis of peripheral blood absolute lymphocyte count to absolute monocyte count >2.1 is a good predictor of long-term survival (70% sensitive, 84% specific, AUROCC 0.82).

Visits should be every 3 months for 2 years, then every 6 months for 3 years, and then annually. Every visit: lymph node, abdominal, thyroid, and skin examination, CBC, and alkaline phosphatase Every visit for 2 years and then every other visit: CXR Annually: TSH level (only if the thyroid was irradiated), mammography for women beginning 10 years after HL diagnosis or at age 40 years, whichever comes first, Pap smear, and influenza immunization Every 6 years: pneumococcal immunization

Long term follow-up data demonstrates excess mortality for those treated at a young age for Hodgkin lymphoma, specifically from cardiac disease and secondary malignancy. Health promotion in relation to reducing other cardiovascular risk factors is important in the longer term management of HL with emphasis on smoking cessation. The risk of secondary breast cancer correlates with the age at which young women received radiotherapy treatment. Current guidelines propose that patients with increased risk are entered into screening programs for early detection of breast cancer . This usually involves MRI and mammography.

A recent analysis of the risk of a second malignancy suggests the risk is decreasing with reduced use of radiation and reduced cumulative chemotherapy doses in patients treated in each subseuqnet decade from the 1970s onwards.
Increasing age is associated with a progressively poorer prognosis, particularly after age 50.
Elderly patients with HL have been found to have a higher incidence of B symptoms, advanced stage, and more aggressive histological subtypes, as well as a poor response to treatment.
Prognosis may be affected by deteriorating T-cell function in the elderly.
Treatment choice must be individualized, taking into consideration the mother's wishes, the severity and pace of the HL, and the length of the remaining pregnancy.
The presenting stage, clinical behavior, prognosis, and histologic subtypes of HL during pregnancy do not differ from those of nonpregnant women.
Diagnosis in the first trimester does not constitute an absolute indication for therapeutic abortion.
If HL presents in an early stage above the diaphragm and appears to be growing slowly, patients can be followed carefully with plans to induce delivery early and proceed with definitive therapy.

Because of theoretical risks that the fetus might develop future malignancies from even minimal scattered radiation doses outside the radiation field, radiation therapy should be postponed, if possible, until after delivery.
Chemotherapy that is administered in the first trimester has been associated with congenital abnormalities in as many as 33% of infants.
In the second half of pregnancy, most patients can be followed carefully and can postpone therapy until induction of delivery at 32 to 36 weeks.
If chemotherapy is required after the first trimester, combination chemotherapy with ABVD appears to be safe.
Steroids are employed both for their antitumor effect and for hastening fetal pulmonary maturity.

HL in children is treated with chemotherapy, but sometimes radiotherapy is also needed. For very localized disease (when the cancer has not spread beyond its original site), radiotherapy alone may be used.
The type and amount of treatment depends on the stage of the disease at diagnosis.
Some children may develop side effects many years later (reduction in bone growth, cardiopulmonary changes, and a small increase in the risk of developing another cancer in later life).
After treatment with chemotherapy, some children (particularly boys) may become infertile.

feature.caption: The Ann Arbor Staging System for Hodgkin's Lymphoma (HL).a
feature.feature_body:
Stage I HL is found in only 1 lymph node area (I).
The cancer is found only in 1 area of a single organ outside of the lymph system (IE).
Stage II HL is found in 2 or more lymph node areas on the same side of (above or below) the diaphragm (II).
The cancer extends locally from the lymph node(s) into a nearby organ (IIE).
Stage III HL is found in lymph node areas on both sides of (above and below) the diaphragm (III).
HL is present in lymph nodes above and below the diaphragm and has also spread to nearby organs (IIIE), to the spleen (IIIS), or to both (IIIE,S).
Stage IV HL has spread widely through 1 or more organs outside the lymph system, such as liver, bone marrow, or lung.
Cancer cells may or may not be found in nearby lymph nodes.
a If HL affects an organ outside the lymph system, but is next to a known area of lymph node involvement, the letter "E" is added to the stage (for example, stage IE or IIE). If it involves the spleen, the letter "S" is added. "Bulky" disease: this term is used to describe tumors in the chest that are at least one-third as wide as the chest or tumors in other areas that are at least 10 cm (about 4 inches) across. It is usually designated by adding the letter "X". Bulky disease may require more intensive treatment. A vs. B: each stage may also be assigned an "A" or "B". The letter "A" is added if the patient does not have certain symptoms that can be caused by Hodgkin's disease. The letter "B" is added (stage IIIB, for example) if any B symptoms are present. The staging classification for HL was adapted from the Ann Arbor Conference and the Cotswolds meeting Additional data from Detailed Guide: Hodgkin Disease How Is Hodgkin Disease Staged? American Cancer Society (ACS).

feature.caption: Treatment of Hodgkin's Lymphoma.
feature.feature_body:
Stage Risk Status Treatment Options
I-II Favorable: no adverse risk factors ABVD for 4 to 6 cycles
ABVD for 2 cycles + IF-XRT (20 Gy or 30 Gy)
I-II Unfavorable: 1 or more adverse risk factors 4 cycles of ABVD plus IF-XRT (20 Gy-30 Gy)
4 to 6 cycles of ABVD
III-IV Favorable: ≤3 adverse risk factors from IPI ABVD for 6 to 8 cycles
ABVD for 6 to 8 cycles + IF-XRT for some patients with bulky disease
III-IV Unfavorable: >3 adverse risk factors from IPI ABVD for 6 to 8 cycles
BEACOPP (increased dose) for 6 cycles
Adverse risk factors (for Stage I-II disease): B symptoms (fever ≥38°C, soaking night sweats, weight loss ≥10% within 6 months), extranodal disease, bulky disease (≥10 cm or >33% of the chest diameter on chest x-ray), 3 or more sites of nodal involvement, ESR of 50 mm/hr or more. International Prognostic Index (IPI) risk factors (for Stage III-IV disease): albumin <4.0 g/dL; hemoglobin <10.5 g/dL; male; age ≥45; Stage IV disease; WBC ≥15,000/mm3; Absolute lymphocytic count <600/mm3 or a lymphocyte count <8% of the total WBC count. IF-XRT: Involved field radiotherapy; ABVD: Doxorubicin + bleomycin + vinblastine + dacarbazine; BEACOPP: Bleomycin + etoposide + doxorubicin + cyclophosphamide + vincristine + procarbazine + prednisone 1.
